quote: Geometrische Bedeutung der Theilung des Lemnis- catenbogens in $a+ib$ gleiche Theile und geome- trische Construction derselben, falls dies möglich ist, vergl. Jacobi Bd 6 S 276.
english: Geometric meaning of dividing the lemniscate arc into a+ib equal parts, and the geometric construction of it, if this is possible; compare Jacobi vol. 6 p. 276.
topic: A list of research problems and plans: shortening Kummer's proof in cyclotomic fields, extending the Pascal hexagon's notable points, Euler's Diophantine problem, division of the lemniscate arc into a+ib parts, transferring Staude's string construction of the ellipsoid, and treating the fields √(a+bi) and ∛α to derive reciprocity laws.

triage.modern_statement: Let φ be Gauss's lemniscatic sine, with ϖ the quarter-period. The lemniscate has complex multiplication by the Gaussian integers Z[i]. For a Gaussian integer α = a+bi, look at the α-division values φ(kϖ/α). These are roots of the 'lemnatomic' division equation and generate an abelian extension of Q(i), which Abel already studied. Hilbert asks two things. (1) What does it mean geometrically to divide the lemniscate arc into 'a+bi equal parts'? (2) When can these α-division points be constructed with ruler and compass? Part (2) depends on whether the relevant Galois group is a 2-group. That is the Gaussian-integer refinement of Abel's theorem on the lemniscate, which says the lemniscate can be divided into n equal arcs by ruler and compass exactly when n is a power of 2 times distinct Fermat primes.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert's note does not appear to have been taken up as a named problem. The constructibility question was settled by Abel's 1826/27 analysis of lemniscate division using complex multiplication by Gaussian integers. M. Rosen gave a rigorous modern proof of Abel's theorem (Amer. Math. Monthly, 1981). D. A. Cox and J. Shurman, 'Geometry and Number Theory on Clovers' (Amer. Math. Monthly 112, 2005), and Cox's Galois Theory (2nd ed., 2012, Ch. 15) treat it with class field theory and complex multiplication. Recent explicit ruler-and-compass constructions, for example dividing the lemniscate into 17 = (1+4i)(1-4i) parts through the (1+4i)-division values, are in Gómez-Molleda & Lario, arXiv:2410.14349 (2024). I did not check Hilbert's Jacobi reference (Werke vol. 6, p. 276).

evidence.claim: Cox–Shurman start from Abel's 1826 discovery about the lemniscate. They prove constructibility results for division points of m-clovers (the lemniscate is m=4) using class field theory and complex multiplication.
Shurman's talk summary says Abel solved the division problem for the lemniscate and that his method contains the beginnings of complex multiplication and class field theory.
Rosen's 1981 proof of Abel's theorem on the lemniscate is regarded as definitive, and later papers give shorter proofs.
The Galois theory of the lemniscate (lemnatomic polynomials, Abel's theorem) is worked out in modern papers and in Cox's Galois Theory, Ch. 15.

Gómez-Molleda & Lario (2024) give practical ruler-and-compass constructions on the lemniscate: halving, doubling, adding and transferring arcs, plus the 17-part division using the Gaussian prime 1+4i and the explicit value φ(ω/(1+4i)).

triage.why: The note asks for the geometric meaning of complex-multiplication division of the lemniscate by a Gaussian integer a+bi, and whether it can be constructed. Constructibility follows from Abel's theory as made rigorous by Rosen and extended by Cox–Shurman: the field of the α-division values is abelian over Q(i), and the points are constructible exactly when its degree is a power of 2. Explicit constructions through Gaussian-prime division values were published in 2024, so the topic is still being written about, but it is a niche, largely expository area rather than an active open problem. It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th. I found no source that answers Hilbert's specific 'geometric meaning' question as he phrased it, and I did not check his Jacobi reference. That is why confidence is medium.
